subject: Which one is more important: AIC or p value in determining the best fittest single season/species occupancy modeling?

messages.author: b18c7e3354ffe63c
messages.subject: Which one is more important: AIC or p value in determining the best fittest single season/species occupancy modeling?
parts:
Hello,
I am a new user of occupancy modeling. I am trying to use the single season/single species occupancy modeling with the unmarked package. I have 53 sites, 72 repeated survey and 5 site covariates. After running some candidate models, the problem I encountered in choosing the best fitted model is
1) the model with the smallest AIC value has not significant site covariates (p>0.1) at all,
2) the model with the significant site covariates (2 in 5 site covariates) (p<0.05) has a little bit larger AIC value than the model with the smallest AIC.
The difference between AIC of these two best model is only 1.72.
Which model I should choose: 1) the model with the smallest AIC or 2) the model with significant site covariates?
Thank you very much for any comments.

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Which one is more important: AIC or p value in determining the best fittest single season/species occupancy modeling?
parts:
I have my standard statistician answer:  It depends.

It depends on more than AIC and a p-value.  Or at least it should.  If it only depended on something calculated from the data that has absolutely no subject knowledge needed, then why would we statisticians need you?

AIC is a relative rather than absolute measure of model quality.  You need to determine if the best model is good enough and not just the best one can do.  That requires subject matter knowledge (and expertise).  Maybe the 2nd best model (irrespective of significant covariates) is a lot cheaper to use or more politically acceptable to use and gives pretty much the same predictions.  I don't know.

The point is that using AIC (and other purely statistical measures) provides reasonable approaches to select models but that isn't the end of it.

OK.  End of sermon.

Jim
